messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaius had always taken pride in his analytical mind, a skill that served him well as a financial analyst. But it was precisely this ability to break down complex situations into manageable parts that now haunted him. Ever since the captivity, he couldn't shake off the feeling of being on edge, even within the safety of his own home. The sound of children crying would send his heart racing, transporting him back to the desolate cell where he'd spent weeks listening to the muffled wails of other prisoners. The auditory trigger would set off a chain reaction, making him feel like he was under threat, as if the walls were closing in on him. As he lay awake at night, sleep vigilance took hold, and his mind would replay the memories of his captivity with eerie vividness. He could smell the stench of sweat and mold that had clung to his skin during those interminable days. The more real than normal quality of these memories only served to underscore the feeling that he'd left a part of himself behind in that cell. But it was the expressions of affection from loved ones, like hugs or gentle touch, that would send him reeling into a vortex of negative appraisals. He felt dehumanized, reduced to an object rather than a person worthy of love and connection. Kaius couldn't shake off the conviction that he'd acted in ways that went against his values during the captivity. The memories of those compromises lingered, poisoning his sense of self-worth. It was as if the silence that followed each triggering event was a deafening reminder that he'd failed to uphold his own moral code. His negative appraisals would, in turn, amplify the triggers, creating an insidious feedback loop. For instance, when children cried on the bus during his daily commute, Kaius's mind would snap back to the cell, and he'd feel a suffocating sense of responsibility for not being able to protect those around him. This threat monitoring – always being on guard – became an exhausting cycle. His relationships began to fray as friends and family grew tired of his distant, hypervigilant demeanor. Even at work, Kaius struggled to focus, constantly scanning the environment for potential threats. The irony wasn't lost on him; as a financial analyst, he was trained to assess risk, but now that skill had become a double-edged sword. As the months dragged on, Kaius's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his daily life. He stopped taking public transportation, citing the "silence" of the bus rides as too much to bear. His social circle dwindled, and he found himself working from home more often than not. The captivity had awakened a deep-seated fear that he couldn't shake – the people responsible had faced no consequences, and this lack of accountability gnawed at him like an open wound. It was only when his estranged wife mentioned her concerns about their young daughter's well-being, citing Kaius's increasingly erratic behavior as a reason for worry, that he realized he needed help. The thought of losing the one person who still mattered to him was too much to bear. With a heavy heart, Kaius scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that they could help him break free from this vicious cycle and find some semblance of peace.
